api: Python and JavaScript SDKs, OpenTelemetry OTLP, public REST API.
cons: Production self-hosting has a real ops footprint: several stateful services, not a single binary
The unit-based billing model is easy to under-forecast, since one multi-step trace consumes many units
No built-in gateway, so caching, routing, and failover need a separate component
Now owned by an infrastructure company, which is a strategic-priority question to revisit rather than a present-day defect
name: Langfuse
pros: MIT-licensed core, genuinely self-hostable, no per-seat multiplication
Usage-based pricing means a ten-person team pays the same as a two-person team for the same traffic
OpenTelemetry-native and framework-neutral, so instrumentation stays portable
Largest open-source community in the category, which shows in integration coverage
files: Prompt versions, datasets, scores, and annotation queues as first-class objects; dataset-based regression testing runs in CI.
value: Tracing, prompt management, evaluation, datasets, human annotation, and cost analytics for LLM applications, with an MIT-licensed core you can run yourself via Docker Compose or take as managed cloud. It is deliberately neutral: built on OpenTelemetry, with native integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, Haystack, and Semantic Kernel, plus thin wrappers for raw provider SDKs. For teams that want production observability without adopting a framework or a per-seat contract, it is the most common landing place.
engine: Self-hosted or managed cloud. OpenTelemetry-native ingest.
status: Active. Acquired by ClickHouse in January 2026; development has continued and the open-source core remains MIT-licensed.
latency: Asynchronous SDK export; no proxy in the request path.

pricing.includes: MIT-licensed core: tracing, prompts, evals, datasets

pricing.limits: Billed per tracing unit, where a trace, observation, or score each count as a unit, so one multi-span trace consumes several
pricing.includes: Higher allowances, longer retention, enterprise features

quality: Broad and mature feature coverage with the largest open-source community in the category. Self-hosting is real but not trivial: a production deployment expects Postgres, ClickHouse, a Redis-compatible cache, object storage, and worker processes.
tagline: The open-source observability default: framework-agnostic, self-hostable, and priced on data rather than seats.
use_cases: Framework-agnostic tracing across a stack that is not standardised on one library
Self-hosted observability where prompts and completions must stay in your infrastructure
Prompt versioning and dataset-based regression tests wired into CI
Cost attribution by model, user, or session
integrations: LangChain, LangGraph, LlamaIndex, AutoGen, Haystack, Semantic Kernel
governance_note: The self-hosted option makes this the straightforward answer when prompt and completion text cannot leave your environment, which is the usual blocker for observability in regulated settings. Running it yourself transfers rather than removes the obligation: the trace store becomes a system holding sensitive text, and belongs in the data map with its own retention, access control, and encryption decisions. The January 2026 ClickHouse acquisition is worth recording in a dependency review, not as a warning but as a fact with a review date, since a widely used open-source tool acquired by an infrastructure vendor has a different long-run trajectory than an independent one, and the MIT core is the hedge that keeps the exit cheap.
training_optout: Self-hosted deployments send nothing outward. Cloud tiers are governed by the vendor agreement; verify current terms.
